title: Microsoft Azure / Microsoft 365 Global WAN Outage — IGP-Purge Command Cascade (Jan 25 2023)
dcName: Global WAN backbone (Madrid capacity-expansion node, AS 8075)

location.region: Global WAN (AS 8075); impact worldwide, majority Asia-Pacific + EMEA
location.az: n/a — backbone WAN, not a single AZ

severity.usersAffected: Not precisely disclosed by Microsoft. Any user served by the affected infrastructure worldwide; majority in Asia-Pacific and EMEA as it hit core business hours. Third-party Downdetector logged thousands of reports — more than 3,900 in India and over 900 in Japan (NPR).
severity.impactUsd: Not disclosed by Microsoft or any regulator.
servicesDown: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps / Identity / Endpoint
Azure Government (reported by news coverage; not itemised in the M365 PIR)

brief: A single IGP-database-purge command, added to a WAN change procedure that was never re-tested, executed network-wide on one router vendor's platform in Madrid — forcing every IGP-joined router in Microsoft's global backbone (AS 8075) to recompute adjacency and forwarding tables and BGP to re-validate all internet prefixes. The resulting packet loss took Azure and most of Microsoft 365 offline worldwide for roughly 5.5 hours, with a second wave triggered 33 minutes later when the same command was run on a second Madrid router.

magnitude.note: Blast radius maximal: the fault was in the global WAN itself (AS 8075), so it degraded client-to-Azure, datacenter-to-datacenter and ExpressRoute paths simultaneously (all three named in Microsoft PIR MO502273), taking down essentially the whole Microsoft 365 suite. Azure Government impact was reported by news coverage but is not itemised in the M365 PIR. Duration 5h35m core (07:08–12:43 UTC) with residual Outlook-on-the-web impact tracked separately (EX502694) into Jan 26 03:50 UTC. Financial score inferred from global productivity impact — no USD figure was disclosed by Microsoft or any regulator, so this is an estimate, not a sourced number.

sequenceOfEvents.event: A network engineer performing a planned task to add WAN capacity in Madrid modifies the IP address on a new router and runs a command to purge the IGP database. On this router vendor's platform the command's default action is global, not local, so it executes across every IGP-joined router.

All IGP-joined routers in Microsoft's global WAN are ordered to recompute their IGP topology (adjacency and forwarding) databases; during the recomputation the routers cannot correctly forward packets.

BGP routers (AS 8075) begin readvertising and re-validating internet prefixes as a second-order effect; ThousandEyes observes multiple Microsoft prefixes withdrawn completely then almost immediately readvertised, precipitating global route-table instability and packet loss.

First wave of SharePoint Online / OneDrive availability loss (of three waves: 07:09–07:22, 07:42–07:47, 08:27–08:29) as User Front End components lose internal connectivity to backend SQL infrastructure.
Microsoft monitoring alerts on-call engineers of a networking issue (within ~3–5 minutes of the command); the team initially begins reviewing DNS configurations.
Microsoft publishes incident MO502273 to the Service Health Dashboard and status.office.com after the admin center is affected.
SPO and ODB are failed off Azure Front Door routing to test for relief; this does not correct the problem.
Monitoring confirms the fault is inside the Microsoft WAN, not DNS — redirecting the investigation to the backbone.

Because the engineer was never informed of the alerts (the modified SOP omitted the checks), the same command is run on a second Madrid router ~33 minutes after the first, creating a second wave of connectivity failures across the network.
Reports confirm multiple services impacted; out of caution Azure reverts a recently deployed IPv6 change suspected as the cause — later confirmed unrelated.
Automated WAN recovery features begin restoring the network just after 08:10; at 08:20 Microsoft identifies the WAN change as the source of the incident.
Telemetry shows the majority of network devices recovered; Outlook desktop-client connectivity recovers around this time.
WAN self-recovers and equipment stabilizes; full prefix reconvergence took roughly 1 hour 40 minutes. Two routers fail to recover automatically, leaving residual intermittent packet loss.
Microsoft Teams recovers at 09:40; SharePoint Online and OneDrive for Business recover by 09:50; some customers begin reporting recovery at 09:51.
Engineers identify additional region-specific packet loss in the India region during the tail of recovery.

Microsoft begins reviewing options to restart affected application pools to clear residual downstream M365 impact; by 11:30 telemetry shows impact no longer occurring for most customers (mailbox application-pool restarts were executed later, ~13:30 UTC).
Majority of Microsoft 365 services recovered, overall service stable, and packet loss returned to normal levels; only a small residual for Outlook on the web remains.
MO502273 closed as resolved after extended monitoring; the residual Outlook-on-the-web impact is tracked separately under EX502694.
Residual Exchange Online impact (a BitLocker / Shared Cache race condition on CAFE components after machine restarts) is fully resolved under EX502694.

rootCause:
Immediate mechanism: At 07:08 UTC on 25 January 2023, a network engineer was adding capacity to Microsoft's global WAN in Madrid. As part of integrating the new routers into the IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol, which connects all routers inside Microsoft's WAN) and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, which distributes internet routing) domains, the modified procedure included a command to purge the IGP database. That command is not vendor-neutral: on routers from two of Microsoft's manufacturers it acts only on the local device, but on the third manufacturer's platform — the one being changed — its default action is global, ordering every IGP-joined router in the entire backbone to recompute its IGP topology database. While the routers recomputed adjacency and forwarding tables they could not forward packets correctly, so this single command silently detonated across the whole global WAN, degrading client-to-Azure connectivity, datacenter-to-datacenter connectivity, and ExpressRoute simultaneously. The IGP storm then forced BGP (AS 8075) to withdraw and re-validate internet prefixes; ThousandEyes observed Microsoft prefixes being withdrawn and near-immediately readvertised, producing global route instability and heavy packet loss.

Latent / organisational root: This was fundamentally a change-management and safeguard failure, not merely "human error." Microsoft's standard operating procedure for this class of change is a four-step gate — validation in the Open Network Emulator (ONE), lab testing, a documented Safe-Fly Review with roll-out/roll-back plans, and Safe-Deployment limiting access to one device at a time. The SOP had been edited shortly before the event to fix problems seen in previous runs, but the edited procedure was never re-tested and shipped without proper pre- and post-checks. Two defences that should have caught the command both had gaps: (1) the real-time Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) system maintains a block-list of globally-impactful commands, but this command's global default behaviour on that specific router model had never been discovered during the high-impact-command evaluation for that platform, so it was never added to the block-list; and (2) the "one device at a time" Safe-Deployment isolation was rendered useless because the single accessible router was still IGP-connected to the whole backbone — device-level isolation gives no protection against a command that propagates through the routing protocol itself. Finally, although monitoring alerted on-call engineers within five minutes, the engineer making the change was never notified (again a consequence of the unqualified SOP edit), so the identical command was executed on a second Madrid router 33 minutes later, causing an avoidable second wave.
contributingFactors: An SOP was edited to fix prior-run problems but was never re-validated in ONE/lab and shipped without proper pre- and post-checks, leaving an error in the live procedure.

The IGP-purge command has different behaviour across the three router vendors — local on two, global on the third — and that global default was never characterised in the high-impact-command review for the changed platform.
The AAA command block-list did not include this command for this router model, so the real-time guardrail let a globally-impactful command run.

Device-level Safe-Deployment isolation (one router at a time) provided no protection because the isolated router was still joined to the backbone via IGP — the blast propagated through the protocol, not through device access.
On-call alerting fired within ~5 minutes but the executing engineer was never informed, so the same destructive command was run on a second router 33 minutes later, creating a second wave.
Timing amplified impact: the change hit during core business hours across Asia-Pacific and EMEA.

Two routers could not auto-recover, and downstream M365 services (SPO/ODB, EXO) needed the WAN restored before they could recover, extending user-visible impact well past the WAN's ~09:35 self-recovery.
Monitoring generated high-volume per-farm/per-feature alerts (SPO/ODB and Teams) rather than quickly detecting a single wider service-wide event, slowing incident triage.

coe.action: Audit and block similar commands that can have widespread impact across all three router vendors for all WAN router roles.
Publish real-time visibility of approved-automated, approved-break-glass, and unqualified device activity so on-call engineers can see who is changing what on network devices.
Implement regular, ongoing mandatory operational training and attestation of following all SOPs.
Prioritise a Change Advisory Board (CAB) review of all SOPs still pending qualification within 30 days, including engineer feedback on SOP viability and usability.
Deploy a fix for the BitLocker / Shared Cache race condition on Exchange CAFE components after restart (residual EX502694 impact).
coe.status: Committed — target February 2023 (99.48% deployed as of Feb 6, 2023)

coe.action: Change detection and routing logic so components in a known-unhealthy state (e.g. degraded Shared Cache) stop receiving production traffic.
Fix an additional low-memory bug that caused unexpected machine reboots (the reboots that surfaced the Shared Cache race condition).
Improve SPO/ODB monitoring logic and alerting thresholds to detect unexpected regional Request-Per-Second changes rather than per-farm noise.
Reduce Teams alerting noise during wide outages and improve incident-management efficiency; improve Teams anomaly-detection latency.

lessonsLearnt: Device-level change isolation is not blast-radius isolation: a command that propagates via the routing protocol (IGP) defeats 'one device at a time' safety because the isolated device is still logically joined to the fabric.
A destructive command's behaviour must be characterised per vendor/platform; assuming a command is local-scope because it is local on two of three vendors is a fatal generalisation.
Any edit to a qualified SOP invalidates its qualification — an un-re-tested SOP change is an untested change and must not fly.
Real-time command guardrails (AAA block-lists) are only as good as their coverage; the high-impact-command evaluation missed this platform's global default, so the guardrail silently allowed it.
Operators executing changes must receive the same alerts as on-call, or they will repeat a destructive action (here, a second router 33 minutes later) before anyone reaches them.
Monitoring that alerts on many narrow symptoms (per-farm/per-feature) instead of the wider event slows detection of a single systemic cause.
Downstream services that depend on the network cannot recover ahead of it; WAN-level faults set a hard floor on M365 recovery time regardless of app-tier health.
improvements: Extend the AAA high-impact-command block-list to cover globally-scoped commands across all three router vendors and all WAN router roles (committed Feb 2023).
Give on-call engineers real-time visibility of automated, break-glass, and unqualified device activity so repeat destructive actions are caught before re-execution (committed Feb 2023).
Mandatory recurring operational training plus attestation of SOP adherence, and a 30-day CAB re-qualification sweep of all SOPs still pending qualification (committed Feb–Apr 2023).
Treat any SOP edit as de-qualifying: force ONE/lab re-validation and pre/post-checks before the procedure can be scheduled.

Resiliency fixes in Exchange Online: fix the BitLocker/Shared Cache race on CAFE, stop routing production traffic to known-unhealthy components, and fix the low-memory reboot bug (committed Feb–Mar 2023).
Tune SPO/ODB and Teams monitoring to detect wide regional/service-wide events quickly and cut alert noise during large outages (committed Mar–May 2023).

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Textbook change-management failure
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This is a textbook change-management failure in which the technical trigger (one CLI command) was trivial but the organisational controls that should have contained it all failed in series: an un-re-tested SOP edit, an incomplete AAA block-list, a device-isolation model blind to protocol-level propagation, and an alerting path that excluded the operator.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Maximal WAN blast radius
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The blast radius was maximal because the fault lived in the shared global backbone (AS 8075) rather than in any single service or region — it simultaneously degraded internet-to-Azure, DC-to-DC, and ExpressRoute paths, so essentially every network-dependent Microsoft 365 and Azure service saw impact at once.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Two distinct outage waves
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: the first at 07:08 UTC and an avoidable second ~33 minutes later when the same command ran on the second Madrid router — a direct consequence of the operator not being wired into the alerting the modified SOP dropped.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery gated by scale
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: automated WAN recovery began just after 08:10 UTC but full prefix reconvergence took ~1h40m, and downstream services could only recover after the WAN stabilised (~09:35 UTC), which is why user-visible M365 recovery stretched to 12:43 UTC.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Long-tail Exchange Online residual
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: A long-tail Exchange Online residual (Outlook on the web / EAS) was a separate, secondary failure mode — a BitLocker/Shared Cache race on CAFE components triggered by mass machine restarts — tracked under EX502694 and resolved 2023-01-26 03:50 UTC.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Impact figures undisclosed
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: No USD or precise user-count figure was disclosed by Microsoft or any regulator; third-party Downdetector data (thousands of reports, >3,900 India / >900 Japan) is the only quantified external gauge of user impact.

technicalDeepDive:
The trigger was a command to purge the IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) link-state database, added to the WAN capacity-expansion SOP for integrating new Madrid routers into Microsoft's IGP and BGP domains. On two of Microsoft's three router vendors this purge is scoped to the local device; on the third vendor's platform — the one being provisioned — the command's default action is global, instructing every IGP-adjacent router in AS 8075 to flush and recompute its link-state/topology database. During that network-wide SPF recomputation the routers could not correctly forward transit traffic, producing immediate, backbone-wide packet loss across client-to-Azure, datacenter-to-datacenter, and ExpressRoute paths.

The IGP event then cascaded into BGP. Because interior reachability changed underneath it, Microsoft's BGP speakers (AS 8075) began re-advertising and re-validating the internet prefixes they carry. ThousandEyes observed Microsoft prefixes — both specific /24s and summary prefixes up to /12 — being withdrawn completely and then almost immediately re-advertised, which destabilised global routing to Microsoft's ranges and drove significant external packet loss for roughly a 90-minute bulk window. Given the size of the network, restoring reachability to every prefix took about 1 hour 40 minutes.

Two safeguards failed to contain it. The real-time AAA system enforces a per-command block-list of globally-impactful operations, but this command's global default on the changed router model had never been surfaced during that platform's high-impact-command evaluation, so it was absent from the list and executed. Separately, Safe-Deployment restricts access to one device at a time; that model assumes damage is bounded by device access, but this command's effect propagated through the IGP adjacency graph rather than through device-to-device access, so single-device access provided zero containment. Compounding it, on-call was alerted within ~5 minutes but the executing engineer was not — a gap introduced by the un-re-tested SOP edit — so the same command was run on the second Madrid router ~33 minutes later, producing a second wave. Automated WAN recovery began just after 08:10 UTC; the WAN self-stabilised by ~09:35 UTC with two routers requiring manual recovery. Downstream, SharePoint/OneDrive front-ends lost connectivity to backend SQL (three sub-waves), Exchange Online connections failed to reach the service, and a separate BitLocker vs Shared Cache race on Exchange CAFE components after machine restarts caused a degraded-cache long tail for Outlook-on-the-web/EAS, resolved under EX502694 at 2023-01-26 03:50 UTC.

fmea.scope: Microsoft's global WAN (AS 8075) during a capacity-expansion change in Madrid — the IGP-purge command and its vendor-specific scope, the AAA command block-list, the change SOP and its qualification, Safe-Deployment device isolation, the alert path to the executing engineer, WAN and BGP reconvergence, incident triage, and the Exchange Online residual. Analysed retrospectively from Microsoft's customer post-incident report (MO502273) and third-party routing analysis held in this dossier. Every corrective action is recorded as committed with a target date in early 2023; only the Exchange fix carries a partial deployment figure, so each revised score is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

modes.item: IGP-database purge command on the third router vendor's platform
modes.function: Clear the IGP database on the router being integrated, without touching other routers
modes.failureMode: The command's default action on this platform is global, so every IGP-joined router in the backbone recomputes its topology and cannot forward packets correctly meanwhile
modes.effect: Backbone-wide packet loss across client-to-Azure, datacenter-to-datacenter and ExpressRoute paths; BGP prefixes withdrawn and readvertised; Azure and most of Microsoft 365 degraded worldwide for a core 5 h 35 min
modes.cause: Vendor-specific command behaviour (local on two vendors, global on the third) never characterised in that platform's high-impact-command evaluation, so the AAA block-list did not include it
modes.prevention: AAA real-time block-list of globally-impactful commands, which lacked this command for this router model
modes.detection: Monitoring alerted on-call within about 3–5 minutes, after impact

rationale.S: Provider-wide outage of the backbone under Azure and Microsoft 365, with no customer workaround: the rubric's 9. Not 10: no hazard to people, no facility lost, and the WAN self-recovered within about 2.5 hours.
rationale.O: Once the command was in the procedure, any run on that platform triggered the global action; a foreseeable condition, weakly guarded because the block-list had not been checked against it.
rationale.D: No interlock stopped the command; monitoring alerted within minutes but only after packet loss began: 'detected after impact by internal monitoring'.

evidence.quote: those from a third manufacturer execute across all IGP joined routers

actions.text: Audit and block similar widespread-impact commands across all three router vendors and all WAN router roles

modes.revisedRationale: A block-list entry turns the slip into a refused command: the command can still be typed but no longer executes (O 6→2), and the refusal is an automated interlock (D 8→2). Recorded as committed for February 2023, not as completed, so the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome. Severity is unchanged: a globally-propagating command that escaped the audit would be just as wide.

playbook.do: Document the scope of the IGP purge command per router platform, and state that the default is global on this platform
Extend the AAA high-impact-command block-list to globally scoped commands on all three router vendors and all WAN roles
Alert on a sudden IGP topology recompute across routers and tie it to the change ticket, so on-call links packet loss to the command
Stop all further changes on the backbone and check the engineer's session history for the commands already run
Post to the Service Health Dashboard that networking is degraded globally, not just a DNS problem
Let the automated WAN recovery run, and recover manually any router that has not rejoined the IGP

modes.item: WAN capacity-expansion SOP and its qualification
modes.function: Ensure every procedure run on the WAN has been validated in ONE and the lab, reviewed (Safe-Fly) and carries pre- and post-checks
modes.failureMode: An SOP edited to fix problems from earlier runs goes live without re-testing or proper pre- and post-checks
modes.effect: An untested purge step reaches a production router, and the edited SOP also omits the checks that would have told the engineer about the alerts
modes.cause: No rule that an edit de-qualifies the SOP until it is re-validated
modes.prevention: Four-step gate: ONE emulation, lab testing, Safe-Fly Review, Safe-Deployment — bypassed for the edited procedure

rationale.S: This is the route by which the provider-wide outage started, so it carries FM-01's severity.
rationale.O: Shipping an edited SOP without re-qualification needs a lapse in an established gate: 'infrequent'. Held below FM-01 so the same event is not counted twice at full weight.
rationale.D: Nothing checked that the edited SOP had been re-qualified before it was scheduled; the gap surfaced through the outage.

evidence.quote: the edited procedure was never re-tested and shipped without proper pre- and post-checks
validation in the Open Network Emulator (ONE), lab testing, a documented Safe-Fly Review

actions.text: Change Advisory Board review of all SOPs still pending qualification within 30 days
Regular mandatory operational training and attestation of following all SOPs
Treat any SOP edit as de-qualifying until ONE/lab re-validation and pre/post-checks are done

modes.revisedRationale: The CAB sweep and attestation make an unqualified SOP less likely to be run (O 4→3). The stronger control, treating every edit as de-qualifying, is an analyst recommendation with no recorded status, so no D reduction is claimed. The CAB review is recorded as committed for April 2023, not completed, so the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Treat any SOP edit as de-qualifying: re-validate it in the lab and confirm pre- and post-checks before it is scheduled
Attest on each use that the SOP in hand is the qualified version and includes the alert-check step
Compare the SOP version in the change ticket with the qualified version and block a mismatch before work starts
Halt the SOP-driven work and pull every task using the edited SOP until it is re-qualified
Run the Change Advisory Board review of all SOPs still pending qualification within 30 days

modes.function: Bound the damage of a change to the single device being worked on
modes.failureMode: Device-level isolation gives no containment, because the accessible router is still IGP-joined to the whole backbone
modes.effect: A command run on one router reaches every IGP-joined router in AS 8075
modes.cause: The isolation model assumes damage travels through device access; this command's effect travelled through the routing protocol
modes.detection: None; the isolation does not observe protocol-level effects

rationale.S: The missing containment is why one router's change became a global WAN outage.
rationale.O: Needs a protocol-propagating command to be run first, an unusual combination; held low to avoid double-counting with FM-01.
rationale.D: No control in the record would reveal that the isolation was ineffective before an event like this.

playbook.do: Treat protocol-propagating commands as global in change review, even on one router taken out of service
Characterise which commands act through the routing protocol for every platform in the WAN, including the new Madrid router
Watch IGP adjacency and forwarding state on routers other than the one being changed during any backbone change
Shut the IGP adjacency of the changed router, or take it off the backbone physically, to stop it re-sending protocol effects
Confirm every router has rebuilt its IGP database before removing the freeze on backbone changes

modes.item: Alert path to the engineer executing the change
modes.function: Stop a change in progress as soon as monitoring sees network impact
modes.failureMode: On-call is alerted within minutes but the executing engineer is not informed, and the same command is run on a second Madrid router
modes.effect: A second wave of connectivity failures about 33 minutes after the first
modes.cause: The edited SOP omitted the checks that would have linked alerts to the change, and on-call had no real-time view of who was changing which device
modes.detection: On-call alerts at 07:11 UTC, not relayed to the change executor

rationale.S: Adds a second wave to an outage already in progress: major degradation, scored below FM-01 so the event is not double-counted.
rationale.O: With no link between alerts and active changes, any change during an alert could continue: 'occasional, weakly guarded'.
rationale.D: Internal monitoring saw the impact, but the signal did not reach the person who could stop the repeat: 'detected after impact'.

actions.text: Publish real-time visibility of approved-automated, break-glass and unqualified device activity to on-call engineers

modes.revisedRationale: If on-call can see the active change while alerts fire, the repeat can be stopped before it runs (D 8→4). Recorded as committed for February 2023, not completed, so the reduction is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Make the executing engineer a recipient of the on-call alerts for the device being changed and require acknowledgement before the next command
Page the named change owner directly when an alert fires inside an open change window
Call the engineer doing the Madrid task by phone and order a stop at the first alert
Use the real-time view of approved, break-glass and unqualified device activity to see who is changing what
Freeze all changes to the WAN until every change owner has confirmed their state to the incident bridge

modes.function: Identify the source of a wide outage quickly
modes.failureMode: Investigation starts on DNS, tries Azure Front Door and an unrelated IPv6 revert, and per-farm alert noise hides the single service-wide event
modes.effect: Fault confirmed inside the WAN at 07:40 and the WAN change identified as the source at 08:20 UTC, about 72 minutes after onset
modes.cause: High-volume per-farm and per-feature alerts in SharePoint/OneDrive and Teams rather than detection of a service-wide event
modes.detection: Network alert at 07:11 UTC; source identification at 08:20 UTC

rationale.S: Lengthens diagnosis rather than causing impact, and the WAN's automated recovery began before the source was named: scored at 6.
rationale.O: Alert noise during wide outages was a standing condition.
rationale.D: Internal monitoring detected the issue after impact but pointed first at the wrong layer.

actions.text: Improve SPO/ODB monitoring to detect unexpected regional request-per-second changes rather than per-farm noise
Reduce Teams alerting noise during wide outages and improve anomaly-detection latency

modes.revisedRationale: Service-wide detection would show a wide event as one event at onset (D 8→6). These actions address M365 monitoring, not the WAN triage path, so the reduction is modest. Recorded as committed for March and May 2023, not completed, so it is a claim about the action, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Tune SPO/ODB and Teams alerting thresholds to detect a regional request-rate shift rather than per-farm noise
Check the change calendar for backbone work before opening a DNS investigation
Test the DNS hypothesis and the Azure Front Door failover in parallel with a backbone review, limiting each to 15 minutes
Ask for a list of changes in the last 30 minutes across WAN, DNS and edge on the incident bridge
Post when the fault is confirmed inside the WAN, so customers stop trying DNS and client-side fixes

modes.function: Restore forwarding and prefix reachability quickly after a network-wide topology recomputation
modes.failureMode: Full prefix reconvergence takes about 1 h 40 min and two routers fail to recover automatically, leaving residual packet loss
modes.effect: Teams recovers at 09:40, SharePoint and OneDrive by 09:50; region-specific packet loss in India at 10:11; downstream M365 impact persists to 12:43 UTC
modes.cause: Size of the network, BGP re-validation of all prefixes, and two routers needing manual recovery
modes.prevention: Automated WAN recovery features, which began restoring the network just after 08:10 UTC

rationale.S: This mode sets how long the outage lasted after the trigger stopped: hours of major-service outage is the rubric's 8.
rationale.O: Needs a network-wide recomputation first, which is infrequent.
rationale.D: Recovery problems such as the two stuck routers and the India packet loss were found by telemetry while impact continued.

playbook.do: Give the platform a manual recovery path for routers that do not rejoin the IGP, and test it
Track routers not yet rejoined and prefix reconvergence as one board, not per service
Hold application restarts until packet loss has returned to normal, since apps cannot recover ahead of the network
Give customers the recovery order: network, then Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive, then residual regions
Keep Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive clients on retry with back-off and avoid restarting clients while packet loss persists
Recover the two routers that did not heal automatically, and chase the India region packet loss

modes.effect: Residual Outlook on the web impact tracked under EX502694 until 03:50 UTC on 26 January

modes.detection: Telemetry after the main recovery; tracked as a separate incident

rationale.O: Needs mass restarts to coincide with the race, an unusual combination.
rationale.D: Seen after impact and handled as a separate incident.

actions.text: Fix the BitLocker / Shared Cache race on CAFE components
Stop routing production traffic to components in a known-unhealthy state
Fix the low-memory bug that caused unexpected reboots

modes.revisedRationale: Fixing the race and the reboot bug removes the two causes (O 4→2). The race fix is recorded as 99.48% deployed as of 6 February 2023 and the others as committed, so the reduction is a claim about the actions, not a confirmed outcome.

playbook.do: Deploy the fix for the BitLocker and Shared Cache race, and the low-memory reboot bug that surfaced it
Alert on CAFE components that report a degraded Shared Cache after restart
Stop routing production traffic to components in a known-unhealthy state
Track residual Outlook on the web impact under its own incident so the main one can close
Restart mailbox application pools in order and confirm each pool is healthy before the next

fmea.impactShort: Global WAN down · 5 h 35 min core

restored.quote: by 11:30 telemetry shows impact no longer occurring for most customers

durationBasis: WAN IGP purge 07:08 UTC → impact no longer occurring for most customers 11:30 UTC 25 Jan

roles.first-responder: Microsoft on-call network engineers alerted by monitoring at 07:11 UTC — not named
roles.incident-commander: No incident commander is named in the record
roles.ops-lead: Microsoft network and service engineers who investigated and tested mitigations
roles.change-owner: The network engineer doing the Madrid WAN capacity task — not named
roles.service-recovery: Microsoft engineers who restarted application pools after the WAN recovered
roles.comms: Microsoft Service Health Dashboard and status.office.com publishers
roles.vendor: The router vendor whose purge command defaults to global — not named
roles.customer: Microsoft 365, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and Outlook users

recorded.quote: runs a command to purge the IGP database
recorded.did: Runs the IGP purge on a new Madrid router at 07:08 UTC; on this platform it acts on every IGP-joined router

recorded.quote: Microsoft monitoring alerts on-call engineers of a networking issue
recorded.did: On-call engineers are alerted at 07:11 UTC, 3 to 5 minutes after the command

recorded.quote: the team initially begins reviewing DNS configurations
recorded.did: Starts by reviewing DNS configurations, which is not where the fault was

recorded.quote: Microsoft publishes incident MO502273 to the Service Health Dashboard and status.office.com
recorded.did: Publishes MO502273 at 07:27 UTC after the admin center is affected

recorded.quote: SPO and ODB are failed off Azure Front Door routing to test for relief
recorded.did: Fails SharePoint Online and OneDrive off Azure Front Door at 07:38 UTC; it does not help

recorded.quote: the same command is run on a second Madrid router
recorded.did: Runs the same command on a second Madrid router at about 07:41 UTC, the engineer not having been told of the alerts

recorded.quote: Azure reverts a recently deployed IPv6 change suspected as the cause
recorded.did: Reverts a recent IPv6 change at 07:44 UTC out of caution; it proved unrelated

recorded.quote: Microsoft begins reviewing options to restart affected application pools
recorded.did: Reviews application-pool restarts from 11:04 UTC; mailbox pool restarts run later at about 13:30 UTC

fishbone.effect: Global WAN outage, 5 h 35 min core
